brief.headline: Continuity Guardian could not reach its model to produce a grounded review
brief.what_broke: 12 session(s) waiting on locks. Root blocker(s): pid 376665 (batch_worker/adhoc_reporting, idle in transaction, txn open 4.1s) blocks 1 session(s); last statement: SELECT 1
brief.who_is_affected: Checkout success 0% over 30s (120/120 failed) vs SLO 95%. Revenue run-rate $18,400/min; about $18,400/min at risk. Verification window 10s. The business tolerates at most 60s of degraded checkout.

options.description: Terminate the root blocker session (batch_worker/adhoc_reporting, pid 376665) to release its locks.
Take no action; let the blocker finish and monitor checkout recovery.
options.cost: about $18,400/min of checkout revenue at risk while waiting

brief.recommendation: The blocking workload adhoc_reporting is not present in the workload registry (BIZ-2), there is no active change-calendar window covering it (BIZ-3), and the cost of interrupting is unknown (BIZ-5). Per the rules, when the trade-off belongs to a human owner, escalate is the correct action. The blocker is idle in transaction for 4.1s, but without registry evidence terminating could have unintended consequences.

audit.report: An untracked workload called adhoc_reporting (pid 376665) held a database lock while idle in transaction for 4.1 seconds, leaving 12 sessions waiting and blocking checkout. Checkout success dropped to 0% over 30 seconds (120 of 120 failed), well below the 95% SLO, with about $18,400 per minute at risk. The Database Guardian first suggested waiting because the blocker looked idle, then switched to escalation after confirming adhoc_reporting has no registry entry, no change-calendar window, and an unknown interruption cost. The Continuity Guardian could not reach its model provider to review the decision, so the incident was escalated to on-call and no recovery action was executed. The business was not back when the negotiation ended after 377.4 seconds.
audit.root_cause: An untracked adhoc_reporting session (pid 376665) held a lock while idle in transaction, blocking checkout and driving success to 0% over 30 seconds.
lessons: Register adhoc_reporting in the workload registry with an owner and interruption cost so the Database Guardian can decide whether to wait or terminate without escalating.
Add a change-calendar window or approved kill procedure for adhoc_reporting batch_worker sessions so an idle-in-transaction blocker can be cleared within the 60-second degraded-checkout tolerance.
Give the Continuity Guardian a local fail-open review path for adhoc_reporting incidents so a model-provider outage does not force escalation and leave checkout at 0% success.
audit.negotiation_critique: The Database Guardian reasoned from the evidence and correctly escalated once probes showed adhoc_reporting was untracked, but it spent its only round investigating instead of executing, and the Continuity Guardian was overridden by the fail-closed invariant when its model provider was unreachable.
follow_ups: Add adhoc_reporting to the workload registry with owner, cost, and change-calendar coverage.
Write and test a runbook to terminate idle-in-transaction adhoc_reporting blockers within 60 seconds.
Configure a fallback or alert for Continuity Guardian model-provider failures so on-call escalation is not automatic.

proposal.rationale: The root blocker (pid 376665) is idle in transaction for 4.1s with last statement SELECT 1, indicating it is not actively holding locks. Per DB-1 there are 12 sessions waiting; TEL-1 shows checkout over the last 15s had 33/60 succeeded (55%) and 27 timeouts; BIZ-1 reports checkout success 77% over 10s (7/31 failed) vs SLO 95%, with $4,155/min at risk. The business tolerates at most 60s of degraded checkout. Given the blocker’s idle state and short transaction age, waiting is lower risk than terminating, and allows time to gather missing evidence (biz.workload_registry, biz.change_calendar, db.protected_settlements, biz.tradeoff).
proposal.expected_effect: No immediate database change; checkout sessions will either recover as the blocker finishes or time out. Monitoring will reveal whether the blocker clears within the 60s business tolerance window.
proposal.risk_assessment: If the blocker persists beyond 60s, SLO breach and continued revenue loss ($4,155/min) may occur. Terminating the blocker could interrupt an ad‑hoc reporting job and potentially cause downstream issues, but waiting avoids that risk at the cost of delayed recovery.
